source_text: Cum ergo et haec exempla magis in persecutionibus eveniant, siquidem magis tunc probamur vel reprobamur, et magis tunc humiliamur vel emendamur, ab eo permittatur vel imperetur necesse est catholice fieri haec a quo et ex parte, scilicet ab illo qui dicit, Ego sum qui facio pacem et condo mala, id est bellum; hoc est enim contrarium paci. Nostrae autem paci quod est bellum quam persecutio? Si persecutionis vel maxime exitus aut vitam afferunt aut mortem, aut plagam aut sanationem, habes auctorem eiusdem: Ego percutiam et sanabo, ego vivificabo et mortificabo. Uram, inquit, illos sicut uritur aurum, et probabo, inquit, illos sicut probatur argentum. Cum enim exurimur persecutionis ardore, tunc probamur de fidei tenore. Haec erunt ignea iacula diaboli, per quae fidei ustio et conflatio administratur, ex dei tamen voluntate. De isto quis dubitare possit, ignoro, nisi plane frivola et frigida fides, deprehendens eos qui timide conveniunt in ecclesiam. Dicitis enim, quoniam incondite convenimus et simul convenimus et complures concurrimus in ecclesiam, quaerimur a nationibus et timemus, ne turbentur nationes. Annon scitis, quod deus omnium sit dominus? Et si velut deus, tunc persecutionem patieris, si vero noluerit, silebunt nationes. Credas utique, si tamen in eum deum credis, sine cuius voluntate nec passer unius assis cadit in terram. Nos autem, puto, multis passeribus antistamus.
orientation: Tertullian is arguing that persecution comes from God, and here he applies the biblical examples of testing and humbling to persecution itself, then answers those who fear gathering as a church.
pass_a_gloss: Since therefore these examples happen more in persecutions, since indeed we are then more tested or rejected, and we are then more humbled or corrected, it is necessary that these things be permitted or commanded to happen universally by him from whom also in part, namely by him who says, I am he who makes peace and creates evils, that is war; for this is contrary to peace. But what is war to our peace if not persecution? If the outcomes of persecution especially bring either life or death, either wound or healing, you have the author of the same: I will strike and I will heal, I will make alive and I will kill. I will burn them, he says, as gold is burned, and I will test them, he says, as silver is tested. For when we are burned by the heat of persecution, then we are tested concerning the steadfastness of faith. These will be the fiery darts of the devil, through which the burning and smelting of faith is administered, yet by God's will. Who could doubt about this, I do not know, unless plainly a frivolous and cold faith, catching those who fearfully assemble in the church. For you say, because we assemble in a disorderly way and we assemble together and many of us run together into the church, we are sought by the nations and we fear, lest the nations be disturbed. Do you not know that God is lord of all? And if God wills, then you will suffer persecution, but if he does not will it, the nations will be silent. You should certainly believe, if however you believe in that God, without whose will not even a sparrow of one ass falls to the ground. But we, I think, are worth more than many sparrows.

choices.why: The adverb means 'generally' or 'universally,' not 'catholic' in the ecclesiastical sense; it modifies how these things happen.
The verb condo means 'to found, establish, create'; 'evils' preserves the plural of mala, which Tertullian immediately glosses as war.
This echoes Ephesians 6:16 language; 'darts' is the traditional rendering of iacula and fits the military metaphor.
Ustio is the act of burning and conflatio the refining by fire; both are needed to keep the metallurgical image of testing gold and silver.
Tertullian uses nationes for the pagan peoples or Gentiles; 'the nations' keeps the biblical resonance and avoids anachronistic 'pagans.'
The ass is a small Roman coin; keeping 'ass' preserves the monetary specificity of the source, matching the literal lane.

pass_b_english: Since these examples also occur more in persecutions, since it is then especially that we are tested or rejected, and then especially that we are humbled or corrected, it must be that these things are universally permitted or commanded by the one from whom they come even in part. That is, by the one who says, "I am the one who makes peace and creates evils" (Isaiah 45:7). That is, war, for war is the opposite of peace. And what is persecution but war against our peace? If the outcomes of persecution especially bring either life or death, either wound or healing, you have the author of it: "I will strike and I will heal, I will give life and I will put to death" (Deuteronomy 32:39). "I will burn them," he says, "as gold is burned, and I will test them," he says, "as silver is tested" (Zechariah 13:9). For when we are burned by the heat of persecution, then we are tested in the steadfastness of our faith. These will be the fiery darts of the devil, through which the burning and smelting of faith is carried out, yet by God's will.

Who could doubt this? I do not know, unless it is a plainly frivolous and cold faith that exposes those who gather in the church fearfully. For some of you say, "Because we assemble without order, and we assemble together, and many of us rush into the church, we are sought out by the nations, and we are afraid that the nations will be disturbed." Do you not know that God is Lord of all? And if he is, as it were, God, then you will suffer persecution; but if he does not will it, the nations will be silent. You should certainly believe this, if you believe in that God without whose will not even a sparrow falls to the ground (Matthew 10:29). But we, I think, stand against many sparrows.

problems.why: 'velut' means 'as it were' or 'if indeed'; 'if he is God' drops the comparative nuance of 'velut' (if he is, as it were, God).
problems.fix: And if he is, as it were, God, then you will suffer persecution
problems.ruling: 'velut' means 'as if/like', not identity; 'if he is God' loses comparative nuance.

problems.quote: But we, I think, are worth more than many sparrows (Matthew 10:31).
problems.source_quote: Nos autem, puto, multis passeribus antistamus.
problems.why: English adds claim of being worth more than sparrows, not present; Latin says we stand against many sparrows.
problems.fix: But we, I think, stand against many sparrows.
problems.ruling: "antistamus" means "we stand against/over"—not "worth more than." Translator changes meaning by importing Matthew 10:31's wording.

edits.old: And if he is God, then you will suffer persecution
edits.new: And if he is, as it were, God, then you will suffer persecution

edits.old: But we, I think, are worth more than many sparrows (Matthew 10:31).
edits.new: But we, I think, stand against many sparrows.

fixed: Changed 'And if he is God' to 'And if he is, as it were, God' to reflect the comparative nuance of 'velut' in the source.

Changed 'are worth more than many sparrows' to 'stand against many sparrows' to match the source 'multis passeribus antistamus' (we stand against many sparrows), removing the added claim of being worth more.

problems.quote: catches those who gather in the church fearfully
problems.source_quote: deprehendens eos qui timide conveniunt in ecclesiam
problems.why: 'Deprehendens' means 'detecting/exposing/convicting,' not 'catches' in the sense of ensnaring; the faith exposes those who come timidly.
problems.fix: that exposes those who gather in the church fearfully
problems.ruling: deprehendens = exposing/convicting, not ‘catches’; translation misrepresents nuance.

problems.quote: sparrow of one ass falls to the ground (Matthew 10:29)
problems.source_quote: nec passer unius assis cadit in terram
problems.why: Adds spurious “of one ass” and distorts the biblical quotation; the Latin says simply “not even a sparrow falls to the ground”.
problems.fix: …without whose will not even a sparrow falls to the ground (Matthew 10:29).
problems.ruling: Source 'passer unius assis' = 'sparrow of one ass' (a penny); translator kept literal 'of one ass' but added Matthew 10:29 which lacks it, misleading readers.

edits.old: catches those who gather in the church fearfully
edits.new: exposes those who gather in the church fearfully

edits.old: not even a sparrow of one ass falls to the ground (Matthew 10:29)
edits.new: not even a sparrow falls to the ground (Matthew 10:29)

fixed: Changed 'catches' to 'exposes' for 'deprehendens', which means detecting/exposing/convicting, not ensnaring.
Removed 'of one ass' from the sparrow quotation; the Latin 'nec passer unius assis cadit in terram' is a biblical allusion meaning simply 'not even a sparrow falls to the ground'.

problems.quote: For you say, "Because we assemble without order
problems.why: Unclear who 'you' is—Fabius? An objector? The reader?
problems.fix: Clarify: 'For some of you say' or identify the speaker.

edits.old: For you say, "Because we assemble without order
edits.new: For some of you say, "Because we assemble without order

fixed: The source 'Dicitis enim' is second-person plural, addressing the congregation generally, not a single named speaker. 'For you say' is already a correct plural address; however, to make the plural explicit and avoid confusion with a singular objector, 'For some of you say' clarifies the address without changing the meaning.

last_rejected.why: Here 'catholice' means 'in a manner befitting the whole/true faith,' not 'universally.'
last_rejected.fix: it must be that these things are permitted or commanded in keeping with the true faith by the one from whom they come even in part.
last_rejected.ruling: catholice = universally/according to the whole, translation acceptable

last_rejected.quote: exposes those who gather in the church fearfully
last_rejected.source_quote: deprehendens eos qui timide conveniunt in ecclesiam
last_rejected.why: 'deprehendens' means 'catching/detecting,' not 'exposes'; subject is the cold faith that catches fearful churchgoers.
last_rejected.fix: that catches those who gather in the church fearfully.
last_rejected.ruling: deprehendens = catching/detecting, 'exposes' is a reasonable rendering

last_rejected.quote: And if he is, as it were, God
last_rejected.why: Source means 'if he is truly God'; 'velut deus' affirms, not hedges with 'as it were.'
last_rejected.fix: And if he is truly God
last_rejected.ruling: velut deus = as if God, translation captures hedging sense

polish.changed: Clarified the speaker of the objection as 'some of you,' smoothed sentence order, removed the em dash, and made pronoun references and quotations easier to follow aloud while preserving every claim and Scripture reference.
